Model-based Constrained Optimization (MBCO) Chi-squared Test

Source: R/00_classes.R
mbco.Rd

This function computes asymptotic MBCO chi-squared test for a smooth function of model parameters including a function of indirect effects.

Usage

mbco(h0, h1, ...)

Arguments

h0

A fitted restricted OpenMx model or medfit SEMFit under the null hypothesis.

h1

A fitted full model of the same class as h0, under the alternative hypothesis.

...

Additional arguments.

Value

An object of class MBCOResult containing

statistic

asymptotic chi-squared test statistic value

df

chi-squared df

p_value

chi-squared p-value computed based on the method specified by the argument type

type

The type of test performed

Details

Two medfit SEMFits (medfit >= 0.8.0). Supply the already-fitted restricted model as h0 and the full model as h1. Only type = "asymp" is supported; alpha is validated as for OpenMx. The adapter compares the fits through stats::anova(h1, h0) and uses the degrees-of-freedom difference. It never refits. Bootstrap types, mixed model classes, OpenMx-only fitting controls (R, checkHess, checkSE, optim, precision) and unused dots are rejected. This route does not require OpenMx.

medfit checks convergence, identical data and observed variables, unweighted fits, and parameter-table nesting. The analyst must establish substantive nesting and a valid chi-square reference distribution; arbitrary nonlinear restrictions do not necessarily have one. An active tested bound or inequality at the null causes an error here because the ordinary chi-square p-value is invalid. Other medfit warnings propagate.

For a product-zero null, medfit::fit_sem() with a*b == 0 fits one branch per factor from clean starts and selects the smallest discrepancy. Pass that fitted null and the full fit to mbco(). medfit is optional: this route needs 0.8.0 or later (GitHub/r-universe); existing ci() integration needs only 0.2.0. No change to the CRAN dependency minimum is implied.

OpenMx comparisons require a finite nonnegative observed statistic and a positive degrees-of-freedom difference: supply the restricted model as h0 and the full model as h1. Equal-df and reversed pairs error before bootstrap sampling. These checks do not establish substantive model nesting.

OpenMx bootstrap methods restore global options on success and error. Set a seed before calling for reproducibility; bootstrap sampling consumes the current RNG stream. The semiparametric method requires positive-definite sample and null covariances. The parametric method simulates each replicate from the fitted h0 with OpenMx::mxGenerateData() (the mvtnorm package is required) and fits h0 and h1 to it in a loop the package runs itself, under the same rules as the semiparametric method; it needs a model with a single raw data set. For both bootstrap types a replicate whose fits did not converge is left out of the null distribution, and the dropped slot of the result counts them. If more than 5% of the R replicates are dropped, the call stops with an error of class RMediation_bootstrap_too_many_dropped (with fewer than 20 replicates no replicate may be dropped). Nothing else is dropped: a replicate with an unrepairable constraint violation (class RMediation_bootstrap_infeasible), a non-finite statistic, or an h1 fit worse than its h0 fit stops the call. The p-value is the proportion of the kept replicates, R - dropped of them, whose statistic is strictly above the observed one, mean(null > observed) over the kept replicates. There is no (1 + k)/(R + 1) correction, so it can be exactly 0 when no kept replicate exceeds the observed statistic.

Testing an OpenMx product null (\(a b = 0\)). The null \(ab = 0\) holds when \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\). A single nonlinear constraint such as ind == 0 can converge to either branch, and the optimizer may return the branch with the larger statistic, which gives a wrong test. mbco_product_null() avoids this: give it the fitted full model and the path labels. By hand, fit one linear null per path (a == 0 and b == 0), run mbco() on each, and report the smaller statistic with 1 degree of freedom (see the example). The smaller statistic is the exact constrained likelihood-ratio statistic for \(ab = 0\). Its chi-square(1) p-value is conservative when both paths are 0 (an intersection-union test; standard theory, not verified here).

Build each h0 from the unfitted model. A constraint refit from the fitted model's estimates can stop at an infeasible point and return a statistic of 0.

Constraint violations and the automatic refit (OpenMx). OpenMx accepts a constrained fit whose constraints are violated by up to its "Feasibility tolerance" (default 0.05), which can understate the statistic (for example 0 where the exact value is 0.4745). Before comparing, mbco() evaluates every equality and inequality constraint of h0 and h1 at the fitted solution. A constraint counts as violated when its scaled violation, |lhs - rhs| / max(1, |lhs|, |rhs|) for equalities and the wrong-side gap for inequalities, exceeds 1e-6. Constraints with other operators are skipped; a constraint that cannot be evaluated is an error naming it.

When h0 is violated, all three types refit it once from its own estimates with "Feasibility tolerance" set to 1e-8, then use the refit model for the observed statistic and the bootstrap, and warn with class RMediation_h0_refit (statistic before and after). The refit slot of the result records tolerance, statistic_before and statistic_after, and is NULL when no refit was needed. Your own model object is not modified. This is the one case where the returned statistic differs from OpenMx::mxCompare() on your fits. If the refit errors, does not converge or leaves the constraint violated, mbco() stops with an error of class RMediation_h0_refit_failed that names the constraint and the reason, before any bootstrap work and for every type: no statistic is returned from a fit known to be invalid. Refit yourself with mxOption(model, "Feasibility tolerance", 1e-8) or use mbco_product_null() for a product null. h1 is checked and warned about (RMediation_constraint_violation) but never refit. Both bootstrap types ("semi" and "parametric") apply the same checks to every replicate: a replicate whose h0 or h1 fit does not converge stops the call at the first one (6 of 100 runs in a simulation with R = 200); a replicate null fit that violates its constraint is refit as above, and one that cannot be repaired stops the call with an error of class RMediation_bootstrap_infeasible instead of entering the null distribution. (Before 1.8.0 type = "parametric" delegated its bootstrap to OpenMx::mxCompare(boot = TRUE), which does neither.)

When h0 came back identical to h1. A refit whose statistic_before is about 0 (|statistic| < 1e-6, h0 and h1 have the same -2LL although a constraint of h0 was violated) also raises a warning of class RMediation_constraint_not_enforced, right after RMediation_h0_refit. It means the constraint may not have been enforced. Two causes give this symptom. OpenMx (2.19.1 and later) silently drops an equality constraint whose Jacobian row is zero at the starting values, so b1 * b2 == 0 started at b1 = b2 = 0 returns the unconstrained fit (OpenMx/OpenMx#433); a violation within the feasibility tolerance looks the same. A fitted h0 keeps no starting values, so mbco() cannot tell the causes apart and the warning does not name either one as the cause. The reported statistic is the refit one. For a product null, skip the problem: mbco_product_null() fits exact single-path nulls and never relies on a nonlinear constraint. The refit and this warning apply to the observed statistic for every type. Both bootstrap types ("semi" and "parametric") repeat the refit on every bootstrap replicate, and a replicate null fit that cannot be repaired stops the call (see above).

Wrong-branch check (OpenMx). A feasible, converged fit of a product null such as a*b == 0 can still sit on the larger-statistic branch (for example a = 0 when b = 0 fits far better), which neither the violation guard nor the refit can see. After the refit, mbco() therefore checks every equality constraint of the h0 it will use. It finds the free parameters the constraint depends on (by perturbing each at the full model's estimates, without parsing the formula), drops the constraint, fixes each of them at 0 in turn, and refits. If a converged fit that still satisfies the constraint has a -2LL lower than h0's by more than 1e-4, mbco() warns with class RMediation_constraint_branch, naming the constraint, the parameter and the gap. It runs once per call for every type, costs one extra fit per involved parameter, and skips (with a message of class RMediation_constraint_branch_skipped) a constraint that depends on more than 5 parameters. The check is advisory: it never changes the result and a failure inside it never fails the call. It only searches fits that fix one involved parameter at 0, so it can show that h0 is not the constrained optimum but not that it is. Use mbco_product_null() to avoid the problem.

Davood Tofighi dtofighi@gmail.com

Examples

if (requireNamespace("medfit", quietly = TRUE) &&
    utils::packageVersion("medfit") >= "0.9.0") {
  d <- as.data.frame(memory_exp)
  d$x <- as.numeric(d$x) - 1
  syntax <- paste("repetition ~ a1*x", "imagery ~ a2*x",
                  "recall ~ cp*x + b1*repetition + b2*imagery", sep = "\n")
  full <- medfit::fit_sem(syntax, d, fixed_x = FALSE, meanstructure = NULL)
  null <- medfit::fit_sem(paste(syntax, "a1*b1 == 0", sep = "\n"), d,
                          fixed_x = FALSE, meanstructure = NULL)
  mbco(null, full) # statistic 0.0831, df 1
}
if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
data(memory_exp)
memory_exp <- as.data.frame(memory_exp) # mxData() does not accept tibbles
memory_exp$x <- as.numeric(memory_exp$x) - 1 # manually creating dummy codes
endVar <- c("repetition", "imagery", "recall") # endogenous variables (not "x")
manifests <- c("x", "repetition", "imagery", "recall")
full_model <- OpenMx::mxModel(
  "memory_example",
  type = "RAM",
  manifestVars = manifests,
  OpenMx::mxPath(
    from = "x",
    to = endVar,
    arrows = 1,
    free = TRUE,
    values = .2,
    labels = c("a1", "a2", "cp")
  ),
  OpenMx::mxPath(
    from = "repetition",
    to = "recall",
    arrows = 1,
    free = TRUE,
    values = .2,
    labels = "b1"
  ),
  OpenMx::mxPath(
    from = "imagery",
    to = "recall",
    arrows = 1,
    free = TRUE,
    values = .2,
    labels = "b2"
  ),
  OpenMx::mxPath(
    from = manifests,
    arrows = 2,
    free = TRUE,
    values = .8
  ),
  OpenMx::mxPath(
    from = "one",
    to = manifests,
    arrows = 1,
    free = TRUE,
    values = .1
  ),
  OpenMx::mxAlgebra(a1 * b1, name = "ind1"),
  OpenMx::mxAlgebra(a2 * b2, name = "ind2"),
  OpenMx::mxCI("ind1", type = "both"),
  OpenMx::mxCI("ind2", type = "both"),
  OpenMx::mxData(observed = memory_exp, type = "raw")
)
## H0: a1*b1 = 0 holds if a1 = 0 or b1 = 0. Fit one linear null per path and
## report the smaller statistic (what medfit::mbco_sem() automates). A single
## nonlinear null ind1 == 0 can converge to the wrong branch (rmediation#35).
## Build each h0 from the unfitted model: a constraint refit from the fitted
## model's estimates can stop at an infeasible point.
null_a1 <- OpenMx::mxModel(
  model = full_model,
  name = "Null a1 = 0",
  OpenMx::mxConstraint(a1 == 0, name = "a1_eq0_constr")
)
null_b1 <- OpenMx::mxModel(
  model = full_model,
  name = "Null b1 = 0",
  OpenMx::mxConstraint(b1 == 0, name = "b1_eq0_constr")
)
full_model <- OpenMx::mxTryHard(full_model, checkHess = FALSE, silent = TRUE)
null_a1 <- OpenMx::mxTryHard(null_a1, checkHess = FALSE, silent = TRUE)
null_b1 <- OpenMx::mxTryHard(null_b1, checkHess = FALSE, silent = TRUE)
res_a1 <- mbco(null_a1, full_model)
res_b1 <- mbco(null_b1, full_model)
res_a1
res_b1
## Test of H0: a1*b1 = 0 (df = 1): the smaller of the two statistics
min(res_a1@statistic, res_b1@statistic)
## The same test in one call: fixes each path at 0 in a copy of the fitted
## full model and returns the binding branch (here b1, statistic 0.0831)
mbco_product_null(full_model, c("a1", "b1"))
} # }
